w: Legend holds that Lord William de Warenne was treacherously slain in a joust on this hill in 1286 - one layer in a long history of sport and recreation here, from medieval tournaments to today's park in Waddon, on Croydon's western edge.
s: A hill said to have hosted a fatal 1286 joust
_facts: Long history of sport and recreation on the hill
Jousting is said to have taken place here in medieval times
Legend holds Lord William de Warenne was treacherously slain in a joust in 1286

w: Six Archbishops of Canterbury lie buried in this Grade I listed parish church in Croydon's Old Town, among them Edmund Grindal, John Whitgift and Gilbert Sheldon. Of the more than 35 churches in the borough, the Minster - Croydon's civic church - remains the most prominent.
s: Parish church holding the graves of six archbishops
_facts: Parish and civic church of the London Borough of Croydon
Grade I listed
Six Archbishops of Canterbury are buried here: Grindal, Whitgift, Sheldon, Wake, Potter and Herring
Most prominent of more than 35 churches in the borough

w: A 499-foot tower on Beaulieu Heights has loomed over Upper Norwood since 1962, replacing the original 1955 lattice mast. It carried London's ITV signal on VHF, fell silent in 1985, then returned in 1997 with a directional aerial built specifically to launch Channel 5 without clashing with continental signals.
s: The 499-foot tower built to launch Channel 5
_facts: Established 1955 with a small lattice tower; present 152m (499ft) tower built 1962
Broadcast London's ITV signal on VHF Band III
VHF television discontinued in 1985; not used regularly again until 1997
1997 directional UHF antenna installed to launch Channel 5 without continental interference

w: Croydon's 1962 concert hall has hosted decades of BBC orchestral, television and radio recordings alongside its theatre and gallery. A 30-million-pound redevelopment shut the whole complex from 2016 to 2019, after which Fairfield Halls reopened to resume its double life as broadcast venue and civic stage.
s: A 1962 concert hall used for BBC recordings
_facts: Arts, entertainment and conference centre opened 1962
Concert hall regularly used for BBC television, radio and orchestral recordings
Closed 2016 for a 30-million-pound redevelopment, reopened 2019

w: Locals call it the 50p Building, or the Weddingcake - a 24-storey Richard Seifert tower from 1970 whose tiered, faceted profile still dominates the view by East Croydon station. It was built for Noble Lowndes Annuities during Croydon's 1960s high-rise boom, decades before London's 2004 plan made such towers routine.
s: The tiered 1970 tower nicknamed the '50p Building'
_facts: Formerly the NLA Tower, nicknamed the 50p Building, the Weddingcake or the Threepenny bit building
Designed by Richard Seifert & Partners, completed 1970
24 storeys, 269 feet (82m) high, next to East Croydon station
Built for original tenant Noble Lowndes Annuities during Croydon's 1960s tower boom

w: Opened in 1809 and shut 27 years later, the Croydon Canal has the dubious distinction of being the first canal in Britain abandoned by Act of Parliament. Its 28 locks carried stone and lime from Merstham workings toward New Cross; the reservoir built to feed it survives today as South Norwood Lake.
s: The canal that became Britain's first to be abandoned
_facts: Ran 9.25 miles from Croydon to the Grand Surrey Canal at New Cross, opened 1809
Closed 1836 - the first canal abandoned by Act of Parliament
Used 28 locks in two flights rather than the planned inclined planes
Its South Norwood reservoir survives as South Norwood Lake

w: For more than 500 years this was the Archbishop of Canterbury's summer retreat, visited by Henry III and Elizabeth I. Grade I listed since 1951, the surviving buildings - now called Old Palace - spent from 1889 to 2025 as home to Old Palace School, a rare medieval palace hiding behind a school gate.
s: The archbishops' summer palace behind a school gate
_facts: Summer residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury for over 500 years
Regular visitors included Henry III and Elizabeth I
Occupied 1889-2025 by Old Palace School, an independent girls' school
Grade I listed since 1951

n: St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood
w: John Loughborough Pearson spent nine years, from 1878 to 1887, raising this red-brick Gothic Revival church above Upper Norwood. Dedicated to John the Evangelist and Grade II* listed, it's a lesser-known showcase of Victorian church-building at work in the suburbs.
s: A Gothic Revival church, nine years in the building
_facts: Grade II* listed red brick Gothic Revival church
Built 1878-1887 by architect John Loughborough Pearson
Church of England, dedicated to John the Evangelist

w: For a century this Coombe Road building has been a hub for Britain's progressive politics - today headquarters to the Communist Party of Britain alongside Croydon's Labour, trade union and co-operative movements. Ruskin House is itself run as a co-operative, with shareholders drawn from across all four.
s: A century-old home for Croydon's progressive politics
_facts: Centre of Britain's progressive movements for a century
Headquarters of the Communist Party of Britain and Croydon's Labour, trade union and co-operative movements
Itself run as a co-operative with shareholders from all four movements

w: From 1809 to 1861, this Addiscombe academy trained young officers for the East India Company's army in India, a counterpart to Woolwich and Sandhurst. Cadets disliked its formal name, the Military Seminary; government took it over in 1858, renaming it the Royal India Military College shortly before closure.
s: The East India Company's own military college
_facts: East India Company Military Seminary, open 1809-1861
Trained officers for the East India Company's army in India
Counterpart to the Royal Military Academy Woolwich and Royal Military College Sandhurst
Taken over by government in 1858, renamed Royal India Military College

w: A Victorian cement warehouse with oak beams held 100 seats and an outsized reputation for new writing - its International Playwriting Festival linked Croydon to partner festivals in Udine and Cyprus. It closed in 2012 when funding dried up and a survey found serious structural faults.
s: A cement warehouse turned 100-seat new-writing theatre
_facts: Oak-beamed former Victorian cement warehouse, 100 seats
Known for new writing and the annual International Playwriting Festival with Udine, Italy and Cyprus
Closed 2012 after funding withdrawal and a survey finding serious structural faults
Home to youth theatre CRYPT and annual collaboration with the Brit School

w: The old Kent-Surrey county boundary runs straight through this 47-hectare park, reclaimed from Victorian sewage farms that once served London and opened to the public in 1989. A duck pond and visitor centre now sit on ground unified into Croydon only in 1965, where the border and the sewage works used to meet.
s: A county-boundary park reclaimed from sewage farms
_facts: 47-hectare park opened 1989 on former sewage-farm land
Historic Kent-Surrey border runs through the site
Wholly within the London Borough of Croydon since 1965
Has a duck pond, visitor centre and car park
